slides.title: JTA Trader — the edge comes from the research loop, not the plumbing
bullets: The edge comes from the research loop, not the plumbing
How a trade flows · how the models keep getting better · what the research has produced
Project walkthrough · 2026-11-17
slides.notes: Automated trading infrastructure is common; what is hard is finding an edge that survives costs and keeps surviving. This deck is about the research and development loop that produces that edge, especially on the machine-learning side, and about what it has produced so far. One slide covers how the system runs. Every number is either MEASURED, read straight from a committed file or result, or ESTIMATED, resting on an assumption, and the tag says which. R means one unit of risk: what a trade loses if its stop is hit.

slides.title: The trading pipeline map: eleven steps, ten model decisions
slides.notes: This is the spine of the deck. Every trade passes through the same eleven steps, from market data to grading. The right-hand column shows where a learned model makes, or is being built to make, a decision: the ML plan cuts the life of a trade into ten decisions, D1 to D10, each owned by one family of models. Two feedback loops close the circle: graded results and retrained models flow back into which strategies and models run, and the paper mirror of each real-money book can demote a strategy back to the demo floor. Per-trade risk sizing is deliberately not a model decision; it stays with the rule-based risk manager.

slides.title: Trade management: entry, in-trade, exit
bullets: 1. Entry — Stop-loss defines 1R; profit target is a real prediction (the TP doctrine).
2. In-trade — Either bracket moves, part-close or close, triggered by live market evidence.
3. Review desk — Every open trade reviewed; options priced from the strategy's own history. 789 reviews on record.
4. Exit + grade — Close reason recorded, trade graded, grade becomes a training label.
slides.notes: Steps 7 to 11 in detail, because this is where the trade is actually managed. At entry every order carries a protective stop, which defines 1R, and a profit target that must be a real prediction, not a placeholder set too far away to ever fill. In the trade, either bracket can move, or the position can be part-closed or closed, but only when something in the live market triggers it: structure, volatility, momentum, regime or a scheduled event. Never the profit alone, never the clock alone. A review function looks at every open trade, prices each option from that strategy's own backtest history, and since 14 November its recommended actions are applied automatically through each account's own risk checks, with a ping to the operator. At the exit the close reason is recorded and graded, and the grade feeds research. Honest status on targets: on real money 7 of 8 routings set a real target at entry, but only 1 of 8 revise it during the trade.

slides.title: The R&D loop: how a model earns, and keeps, its place
bullets: 1. Diagnose — Why is the champion not better? Name the lever: label, features, threshold, exit.
2. Pre-register — Test, statistic and pass mark written down before the run.
3. Test — Held-out data, full cost stack, challenger vs champion on the same trades.
4. Decide — Pass → real money + mirror. Fail → back to Diagnose.
5. Monitor — Mirror net-negative after costs → demo floor, keep iterating.
slides.notes: This is the core of the project. Every strategy and every model sits in the same loop. Start from a diagnosis of why the current version is not better. Write down the test and its pass mark before running it. Run it on data held out from tuning, charged with the full cost of trading. Compare the challenger with the champion, the version in use, on the same trades and the same costs. Pass, and it goes straight to real money with a paper mirror. Fail, and the result is not thrown away: it becomes the next diagnosis. A live model whose mirror goes net-negative after costs drops back to the demo floor and keeps generating data while it is improved. Retirement needs evidence that no lever helps, never a fixed number of attempts.
slides.footnote: Rules: docs/plans/OPERATING-PLAN-2026-09-21.md § 2 (no step between a backtest pass and real money, 2026-11-12; the held-out pass governs real money) and § “What does not pass goes back into research”.

slides.title: One real cycle: the equity entry model, November 2026
slides.notes: A worked example of the loop on a model trading real money today. The equity entry model, internally Foxhound-4, passed its held-out confirmation and was promoted to real money on 8 November. Its diagnosis said it trades in clusters during volatile months. So a test was pre-registered: does the model really predict direction, or is it ranking trades by how cheap they are to trade relative to their risk? The answer, graded on 17 November, was the second: its score tracks cost per unit of risk, and once volatility is neutralised it has almost no directional signal. The test's two alternative labels did not beat it, so it failed. That failure named the next lever: a cost-neutral training target, registered the same day. The live model keeps trading while the challenger is tested; nothing waits on a calendar.

slides.title: The model families, placed on the map
slides.notes: Each family sits on the step where it decides. Most are gradient-boosted decision trees: many small trees added together, each correcting the last; they suit tabular market data and retrain fast. The filter is a deliberately simple logistic regression. Three decisions have no model yet and run on rules, which we state rather than hide.
slides.footnote: MEASURED from model artifacts (ml/served, ml/candidates, ml/overlay, ml/configs) and ml/served/SERVED_MODELS.yaml. The D8 exit head's artifact lives on the trainer; its type is not verified here.

slides.title: Step 3 · Foxhound: how an entry model decides
bullets: 1. Reads — ~20 inputs: returns 1h–1wk, volatility, range position.
2. Trees — 300 gradient-boosted trees (equity: 5-model average).
3. Predicts — Net R of a standard 2-stop / 3-target trade.
4. Acts — Score above threshold → trade. Else nothing.
slides.notes: Every four hours, for each market, the model reads about twenty numbers on recent moves, volatility and range position, and predicts the net R of a standard trade: stop two average ranges away, target three, held up to a day. Above a threshold it trades; otherwise it does nothing. The crypto model learned from about 660 thousand past decisions on 60 coins. The equity model averages five models on 173 funds, long only. Not every challenger wins: the second crypto version failed and stays on paper.
slides.footnote: Crypto, live: +0.037R per trade, n 907, held out. Crypto v2: -0.12R, n 320, failed → paper. MEASURED: ml/served/ml_decision_entry_v1/model.json, ml/candidates/ml_entry_eq_v3_struct_ens5/model.json, ml/served/SERVED_MODELS.yaml.

slides.title: Step 4 · Collie and Beagle: when to step aside
bullets: 1. Collie reads — Returns, volatility, hour, weekday + 6 forecast features.
2. Collie decides — Regime class → strategy steps aside where it loses.
3. Beagle reads — 9 trend and volatility features per signal.
4. Beagle decides — Weak signal → halve size. Strong → take it.
slides.notes: Two families act between a proposal and an order. Collie classifies the market regime, calm or volatile, trending or not, from returns, volatility, time of day and six forecast features from a small pretrained forecaster; a strategy can be switched off only in the regimes where it loses. Beagle scores each signal from two trend strategies and halves the size of weak ones; it passed a no-harm test on 1,830 historical trades. An 11 November inventory proposed retiring most registered models that nothing uses: the loop pruning itself.
slides.footnote: Beagle no-harm test: n 1830, pass. Inventory 2026-11-11: 106 models; keep 15, review 19, retire 72. MEASURED: ml/overlay/overlay_td.json, ml/configs/btc-regime-15m-lgbm-fc-pcv-v2.yaml, comms/ml_consolidation/.

slides.title: Steps 7 and 9 · Labrador: managing the open trade
bullets: 1. Check-in — At 5 points in the trade, read 29 inputs.
2. Classify — Gradient-boosted classifier over 18 target levels.
3. Compare — Expected net R of each level vs the current target.
4. Act — Clearly better → extend the target. Never pull it in.
slides.notes: Labrador re-predicts where a live trade is likely to get to at five check-ins, choosing among 18 target levels, and may only extend the target, never pull it in. Its measured gain is small but positive. The exit head decides whether to close now; it failed out of sample on two of three markets, so it closes trades only on the demo floor. Showing the small and failed results is part of the discipline.

slides.title: Produced so far 3 — research throughput, and how much fails
bullets: 1927 questions done — 411 passed · 1086 failed · 267 indeterminate. 27% pass rate on decisive results.
54 strategy backtests — 32 passed, 22 failed, after the full cost stack. Scalps: 0 of 7 passed.
319 questions queued — Each written down with its data, test and pass mark before it runs. A dispatcher runs them on cloud runners.
slides.notes: The volume behind the results. The research queue has 1927 completed questions. Of the graded ones, 411 passed their pre-registered rule and 1086 failed, with 267 indeterminate because the sample was too small to call. That is a pass rate of 27% on decisive results. Strategy evidence tells the same story: of 54 measured backtests, 32 passed. The short-term scalp family passed 0 of its 7 tests and is not on real money. Most ideas fail, and the system is built so that they fail cheaply, offline, before any money is at risk.
slides.footnote: MEASURED: research/queue/*.yaml (status + grading.verdict; 153 done units carry no verdict); comms/strategy_evidence/*.json. Commit 8545532c7.

slides.title: How it runs automatically, in one slide
bullets: Venues — Crypto perpetual futures, US funds and futures, and prop-firm accounts. 11 of 14 accounts sending orders.
Two switches — Account: live or dry run. Strategy: live or shadow. No hidden third switch; never self-halts.
Run by agents — AI agent sessions do the research and reviews; 23 operator-granted mandates let evidence-backed decisions proceed.
slides.notes: The infrastructure, briefly. The trader runs around the clock on cloud servers, on crypto, US funds and futures venues, plus prop-firm accounts. 11 of 14 accounts are switched on to send orders. Exactly two switches decide whether something trades: one per account, one per strategy. It never switches itself off: failures are contained to one trade or job and retried. Day to day, AI agent sessions run the research, reviews and bookkeeping under 23 standing mandates the operator has granted; agents may propose a mandate, only the operator grants one. Real money excludes fossil-fuel funds by the operator's policy.
slides.footnote: MEASURED: config/accounts.yaml, config/mandates.yaml; rules docs/CLAUDE-RULES-CANONICAL.md § Prime Directive, CLAUDE.md § The two execution gates; config/values_exclusions.yaml.

slides.title: Roadmap: the next ML milestone at each decision
slides.notes: Where the loop goes next, decision by decision. The entry model's next challenger tests a cost-neutral target. The regime family is being pruned to the heads that beat their baseline. The empty slots each have a first question: predicted brackets at entry, combining several signals on one market, cheaper order placement, and whether a learned review of closed trades detects a fading strategy earlier than a simple statistical alarm. Alongside: more ML in the live loops, the trading desk made production-ready, and more labelled outcomes, which are the binding constraint. The deck ends here: no request, just the plan.
